title: The Hidden Nodule: Knowing When to Stop
subtitle: Risk stratification and de-escalation in an incidental thyroid nodule
description: Which test decides whether biopsy is needed at all, ranking sonographic patterns, size thresholds that follow from pattern, FNA technique, indeterminate cytology, what a molecular test can and cannot tell you, the 2025 ATA surgical extent, and why common occult disease still does not justify prophylactic dissection.

steps.title: Step 1/10: The Report She Brings You
steps.scenario: A 45-year-old woman is found to have a 1.8 cm right thyroid nodule incidentally on neck ultrasound during an employee health check. She has no dysphagia, hoarseness, neck pain, or compressive symptoms. She has no history of neck irradiation and no family history of thyroid cancer. She brings the report to your clinic.
steps.media: Load image: Outpatient thyroid examination, physician palpating the anterior neck. Caption: none.
steps.question: Alongside a dedicated thyroid ultrasound, which single result determines whether this nodule needs a biopsy at all?

options.text: (A) Serum thyroid-stimulating hormone
(B) Serum calcitonin
(C) Serum thyroglobulin
(D) Anti-thyroid peroxidase antibody

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

TSH is the branch point, not a baseline. A suppressed TSH raises the possibility of an autonomously functioning nodule, which is very rarely malignant, and sends you to scintigraphy rather than to a needle. A normal or high TSH keeps you on the sonographic pathway. Her result: TSH 1.4 microIU/mL, normal.

Why the others fail:
(B) Calcitonin is the strongest of the three. Several European groups screen routinely to detect medullary carcinoma early, and the ATA has not recommended routine screening, citing cost-effectiveness and false positives. It is a defensible position, but it is not what decides whether this nodule needs a needle.
(C) Thyroglobulin has no role in evaluating a nodule. Its place is post-thyroidectomy surveillance. This is the most common reflex error on this pathway, and it costs the patient a test that cannot change any decision.
(D) Anti-TPO identifies autoimmune thyroiditis. It changes neither the malignancy risk of this nodule nor the decision to biopsy it.

Keypoint: TSH decides whether the nodule needs a needle at all; every other serum test at this stage is either downstream or irrelevant.

Reference: Haugen BR, Alexander EK, Bible KC, et al. 2015 American Thyroid Association Management Guidelines for Adult Patients with Thyroid Nodules and Differentiated Thyroid Cancer. Thyroid. 2016;26(1):1-133. doi:10.1089/thy.2015.0020.

steps.title: Step 2/10: The Result You Did Not Get
steps.scenario: Her TSH is normal, so you continue. Before you do, consider the path you did not take.
steps.question: Had her TSH returned suppressed at 0.05 microIU/mL, what would change?

options.text: (A) Radioiodine scintigraphy first; a hyperfunctioning nodule rarely requires FNA
(B) Proceed to FNA regardless, since a suppressed TSH raises the malignancy risk
(C) Start an antithyroid drug and repeat the ultrasound in six months before any biopsy
(D) Obtain a contrast-enhanced neck CT to assess substernal extension before biopsy

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

A hyperfunctioning nodule is seldom malignant, so scintigraphy answers the question that a needle would only complicate. Establish function before you sample.

Why the others fail:
(B) This inverts the relationship. Malignancy risk rises with higher TSH, not lower. The reversal is common, and it comes from reading suppressed as abnormal and abnormal as dangerous.
(C) Treats the biochemistry and abandons the nodule. The functional and the structural questions are separate, and both need answering.
(D) Carries a specific harm worth owning as a surgeon. An iodinated contrast load saturates the thyroid and can delay scintigraphy or radioiodine therapy for weeks to months. Cancelling the scan afterwards does not undo it.

Keypoint: higher TSH means higher risk, and contrast given before functional status is known is a mistake you cannot take back.

Reference: Haugen BR, Alexander EK, Bible KC, et al. 2015 American Thyroid Association Management Guidelines for Adult Patients with Thyroid Nodules and Differentiated Thyroid Cancer. Thyroid. 2016;26(1):1-133. doi:10.1089/thy.2015.0020.

steps.title: Step 3/10: Ranking the Patterns
steps.scenario: You perform the ultrasound yourself rather than reading the report. Sonographic risk stratification is a pattern-based judgment, not a checklist of individual features.
steps.media: Load image: Longitudinal and transverse grayscale images of a right thyroid nodule, unannotated. Caption: 'Right lobe, 12 MHz linear probe.'
steps.question: Which of these four sonographic descriptions carries the highest malignancy risk?

options.text: (A) Solid, hypoechoic, irregular margins, punctate echogenic foci, taller than wide
(B) Solid, isoechoic, smooth margins, with a thin peripheral hypoechoic halo
(C) Mixed cystic and solid, with an eccentric solid component and smooth margins
(D) Spongiform, with microcystic spaces occupying more than half the volume

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

Sonographic risk is a pattern judgment, not a tally of individual features. Marked hypoechogenicity, irregular or lobulated margins, microcalcifications, and a taller-than-wide shape together define the high-suspicion pattern, with a malignancy risk above 70 to 90 percent. Her nodule matches this pattern, measures 1.8 cm, and there are no sonographically abnormal cervical nodes.

Why the others fail:
(B) Intermediate suspicion, roughly 10 to 20 percent. A solid isoechoic nodule with smooth margins is not benign, it is lower risk.
(C) Low suspicion, roughly 5 to 10 percent. The eccentric solid component is what keeps this above the very-low tier.
(D) Very low suspicion, under 3 percent. Spongiform architecture is the most reassuring pattern short of a purely cystic nodule.

The percentages above are the ATA sonographic pattern figures. ACR TI-RADS is a separate system with its own point-based levels and its own biopsy thresholds, so work from one or the other rather than blending them.

Keypoint: every sonographic pattern carries a risk figure, and the skill is ranking them rather than sorting into benign and malignant.

Reference: Haugen BR, Alexander EK, Bible KC, et al. 2015 American Thyroid Association Management Guidelines for Adult Patients with Thyroid Nodules and Differentiated Thyroid Cancer. Thyroid. 2016;26(1):1-133. doi:10.1089/thy.2015.0020. Tessler FN, Middleton WD, Grant EG, et al. ACR Thyroid Imaging, Reporting and Data System (TI-RADS): White Paper of the ACR TI-RADS Committee. J Am Coll Radiol. 2017;14(5):587-595. doi:10.1016/j.jacr.2017.01.046.

steps.title: Step 4/10: The Threshold Follows the Pattern
steps.scenario: You have a high-suspicion nodule measuring 1.8 cm.
steps.question: At what size does FNA become indicated for a nodule with this sonographic pattern?

options.text: (A) 1 cm or larger
(B) 1.5 cm or larger
(C) 2 cm or larger
(D) Any size, since the pattern alone justifies sampling

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

The threshold is not a single number, it moves with the sonographic pattern. High and intermediate suspicion, 1 cm. Low suspicion, 1.5 cm. Very low suspicion, 2 cm, with observation a reasonable alternative. Purely cystic nodules do not require FNA at all. Her 1.8 cm high-suspicion nodule clears the threshold.

Why the others fail:
(B) The right number attached to the wrong pattern. 1.5 cm is the low-suspicion threshold.
(C) Also a real threshold, for very low suspicion nodules, where observation is an equally reasonable alternative to sampling.
(D) Sounds cautious, and is how subcentimeter nodules get biopsied, microcarcinomas that were never going to matter get found, and a healthy 45-year-old is committed to an operation and a lifetime of surveillance.

Keypoint: thresholds exist because more sampling is not the same as better care.

Reference: Haugen BR, Alexander EK, Bible KC, et al. 2015 American Thyroid Association Management Guidelines for Adult Patients with Thyroid Nodules and Differentiated Thyroid Cancer. Thyroid. 2016;26(1):1-133. doi:10.1089/thy.2015.0020.

steps.title: Step 5/10: The Student and the Big Needle
steps.scenario: The patient consents to ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration. While you set up, a medical student hands you an 18-gauge core needle and says: "If we get cyst fluid, we should send all of it for cytology to improve the yield."
steps.media: Load video: Ultrasound-guided FNA, transverse approach, needle tip visualized within the nodule. 10 seconds, muted.
steps.question: Which statement about needle choice and cystic fluid is most correct?

options.text: (A) Use a 25 to 27 gauge needle; aspirating cyst fluid may relieve symptoms, but cytology of the fluid itself adds little
(B) Use a 25 to 27 gauge needle, and send the cyst fluid for cytology since it may carry diagnostic cells
(C) Use an 18 gauge core needle as first-line, since it lowers the nondiagnostic rate
(D) Use a 25 to 27 gauge needle, and proceed to diagnostic lobectomy if the first pass is nondiagnostic

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

Standard technique is a 5 to 10 mL syringe with a 25 to 27 gauge needle and roughly five seconds of needle undulation within the lesion. Fine needles bleed less, and blood dilution is a major cause of nondiagnostic samples, which is why bigger is not better here.

Why the others fail:
(B) Cyst fluid is usually acellular or full of macrophages. Aspirating it can shrink the nodule and relieve symptoms, but the diagnostic answer lives in the solid component, which should be sampled under direct ultrasound guidance.
(C) Core needle biopsy has a real role in selected situations, including repeatedly nondiagnostic nodules and suspected lymphoma or anaplastic disease where tissue architecture matters. It is not a first-line tool for a routine nodule.
(D) A nondiagnostic FNA is managed with a repeat FNA after an interval. Going to an operation for a diagnosis you have not yet tried twice to obtain is how a benign nodule becomes a hemithyroidectomy.

Keypoint: the commonest cause of a nondiagnostic thyroid aspirate is blood, which argues for a smaller needle and a second attempt rather than a bigger needle or a knife.

Reference: Haugen BR, Alexander EK, Bible KC, et al. 2015 American Thyroid Association Management Guidelines for Adult Patients with Thyroid Nodules and Differentiated Thyroid Cancer. Thyroid. 2016;26(1):1-133. doi:10.1089/thy.2015.0020.

steps.title: Step 6/10: Bethesda III
steps.scenario: One week later the cytology returns as atypia of undetermined significance, Bethesda category III. The patient calls, anxious, and asks what this means and what happens next.
steps.media: Load image: Cytology slide, Diff-Quik stain, follicular cells with mild nuclear atypia. Caption: 'Fine needle aspirate, right thyroid nodule.'
steps.question: What is the appropriate next step?

options.text: (A) Repeat FNA, molecular testing, or continued surveillance, chosen according to sonographic and clinical risk
(B) Diagnostic lobectomy, since indeterminate cytology cannot be resolved by further sampling
(C) Total thyroidectomy, since the malignancy risk of Bethesda III exceeds 50 percent
(D) Reassurance and a repeat ultrasound in twelve months

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

Bethesda III carries a risk of malignancy of 13 to 30 percent, with a mean of 22 percent, and that number is the whole answer. It is high enough that discharging her for a year with a high-suspicion nodule is unsafe. It is low enough that operating commits most of these patients to a procedure they did not need. Given her sonographic pattern, molecular testing is the reasonable next move.

Why the others fail:
(B) This was standard practice for years and remains the default in many units. Repeat sampling and molecular testing both resolve a substantial proportion of these nodules without an operation.
(C) A base-rate error. It treats an indeterminate result as though it were a positive one. Seven or eight of every ten patients in her position do not have cancer, and a total thyroidectomy commits all ten to lifelong hormone replacement.
(D) Unsafe in this particular patient. Twelve months of watchful waiting might be defensible for an indeterminate result in a very-low-suspicion nodule. It is not defensible alongside the high-suspicion pattern documented earlier.

Two points of current nomenclature. The third edition retired the dual designations, so AUS/FLUS, unsatisfactory, and suspicious for a follicular neoplasm no longer appear in reports, and AUS is now subcategorised into nuclear atypia and other, which carry materially different implied risks. Be ready for a challenge on the range as well: published institutional series report AUS malignancy rates above it, some over 38 percent, largely reflecting referral-centre case mix.

Keypoint: an indeterminate result is not a positive one, and the sonographic pattern is what tells you which indeterminate patient you are looking at.

Reference: Ali SZ, Baloch ZW, Cochand-Priollet B, Schmitt FC, Vielh P, VanderLaan PA. The 2023 Bethesda System for Reporting Thyroid Cytopathology. Thyroid. 2023;33(9):1039-1044.

steps.title: Step 7/10: What a Molecular Test Actually Buys You
steps.scenario: You send the aspirate for molecular testing. Before the result comes back, be clear with yourself about what each possible answer would mean.
steps.media: Load image: Molecular test report, result panel redacted. Caption: 'Report header only.'
steps.question: Which statement best describes what a benign molecular result would do for this patient?

options.text: (A) It has a high negative predictive value, allowing surveillance rather than diagnostic surgery in most patients
(B) It confirms the nodule is benign, and no further ultrasound follow-up is needed
(C) It reliably predicts the extent of surgery required if malignancy is later found
(D) Its predictive performance is the same regardless of the sonographic risk pattern

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

The commercially available panels are built as rule-out tests. Their negative predictive value in indeterminate cytology is high, which is what allows a patient to be observed instead of operated on. Their positive predictive value is considerably lower, so a positive result is a reason to plan surgery, not a diagnosis in itself.

Why the others fail:
(B) Overreads a negative test into a discharge. A benign molecular result supports surveillance, and surveillance means continued ultrasound, not the end of follow-up.
(C) Confuses a diagnostic tool with a staging one. Molecular results inform whether to operate; extent of surgery is decided by tumor size, extrathyroidal extension, and nodal status.
(D) The one senior learners get wrong. Predictive values depend on pre-test probability. A benign result in a very-low-suspicion nodule is strongly reassuring; the same result in the high-suspicion nodule this patient has is less so, because disease prevalence in that group is higher. The assay does not know what the ultrasound looked like. You do, and you have to combine them.

Keypoint: a test result means something different depending on who it was run on, and the ultrasound is what tells you who that is.

Reference: Haugen BR, Alexander EK, Bible KC, et al. Thyroid. 2016;26(1):1-133. doi:10.1089/thy.2015.0020, section on molecular testing in indeterminate cytology. Performance figures should be taken from the validation data for the specific assay and version in use.

steps.title: Step 8/10: Reading the Panel
steps.scenario: The molecular report returns positive. You now need to interpret which alteration was found and what weight to give it.
steps.question: Which single alteration, if detected, is most specific for papillary thyroid carcinoma?

options.text: (A) BRAF V600E
(B) An RAS point mutation
(C) A TERT promoter mutation
(D) PAX8/PPARG rearrangement

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

BRAF V600E is close to diagnostic. It occurs essentially only in papillary carcinoma and in the anaplastic carcinomas derived from it, and is not found in benign thyroid disease, so a positive result on an adequate sample effectively settles the diagnosis before surgery. Her result: BRAF V600E positive. This is papillary thyroid carcinoma.

Why the others fail:
(B) RAS is the classic trap. RAS mutations are common in follicular-variant papillary carcinoma, but they also appear in benign follicular adenomas and in NIFTP. High sensitivity, poor specificity, and a positive RAS result does not confirm cancer.
(C) TERT promoter mutations are prognostic rather than diagnostic. They mark aggressive behavior, particularly alongside BRAF, and they change your risk conversation rather than your diagnosis.
(D) PAX8/PPARG rearrangement points toward follicular neoplasms, not papillary carcinoma.

Keypoint: sensitivity tells you what a negative result rules out and specificity tells you what a positive result rules in, and RAS versus BRAF is the cleanest illustration of that difference in thyroid pathology.

Reference: Haugen BR, Alexander EK, Bible KC, et al. Thyroid. 2016;26(1):1-133. doi:10.1089/thy.2015.0020, section on molecular markers in indeterminate cytology.

steps.title: Step 9/10: How Much Thyroid Comes Out
steps.scenario: Papillary thyroid carcinoma, 1.8 cm, clinical T1b N0 M0. No gross extrathyroidal extension on ultrasound, the contralateral lobe is sonographically normal, and there are no suspicious lymph nodes. She asks whether the whole thyroid has to come out.
steps.media: Load image: Side-by-side diagram of thyroid lobectomy and total thyroidectomy. Caption: none.
steps.question: According to the 2025 ATA guidelines, what is the recommended surgical extent?

options.text: (A) Lobectomy
(B) Total thyroidectomy, to permit radioiodine and thyroglobulin surveillance
(C) Total thyroidectomy, because BRAF V600E positivity independently warrants it
(D) Active surveillance without surgery, given the tumor is under 2 cm

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

The 2025 ATA guidelines state that for tumors smaller than 2 cm without gross extrathyroidal extension or metastases, lobectomy should be the first treatment of choice when surgery is indicated, provided there are no bilateral tumors or other reasons to remove the contralateral lobe. This is a strong recommendation with moderate certainty of evidence. Lobectomy may also be the recommended initial strategy for low-risk unilateral tumors of 2 to 4 cm. The shift is real: in 2009 total thyroidectomy was recommended for nearly all cancers above 1 cm, in 2015 lobectomy became an option, and in 2025 it became the recommendation.

Why the others fail:
(B) Reverses the logic by choosing a larger operation in order to enable an adjuvant treatment she does not need. Radioiodine and thyroglobulin surveillance are consequences of the surgical decision, not reasons for it.
(C) A belief many surgeons hold. BRAF V600E positivity alone does not change the recommended extent in an otherwise low-risk tumor, though it may enter the risk conversation.
(D) The right concept applied to the wrong size. Active surveillance is discussed for low-risk tumors of 1 cm or less, alongside lobectomy and percutaneous ablation, not for a 1.8 cm cT1b.

Note the scope of this document. The 2025 guideline covers differentiated thyroid cancer only, and thyroid nodules were removed from it, so the workup earlier in this case rests on the 2015 guideline instead.

Keypoint: the operation is chosen for the tumor in front of you, not for the surveillance strategy you imagine afterwards.

Reference: Ringel MD, Sosa JA, Baloch Z, et al. 2025 American Thyroid Association Management Guidelines for Adult Patients with Differentiated Thyroid Cancer. Thyroid. 2025;35(8):841-985, Recommendation 15.

steps.title: Step 10/10: While You Are In There
steps.scenario: You have agreed on a right lobectomy. In the pre-operative visit her husband asks: "Since you are already operating, can you take out the lymph nodes in that area too, just to be safe?"
steps.media: Load image: Central compartment level VI anatomy, with recurrent laryngeal nerve and parathyroid glands labeled. Caption: 'Level VI.'
steps.question: For this clinically node-negative T1b tumor, what do you recommend?

options.text: (A) Recommend against it, since it does not improve long-term outcomes in cN0 T1 to T2 disease and adds nerve and parathyroid risk
(B) Perform an ipsilateral central dissection, since the morbidity is acceptable and it refines recurrence risk staging
(C) Perform a bilateral central dissection, since occult nodal disease is present in a large proportion of these patients
(D) Defer, and perform a completion dissection later if surveillance thyroglobulin rises

steps.feedback:
Correct answer: A

The 2025 ATA guidelines more strongly discourage prophylactic central compartment dissection for clinically node-negative T1 to T2 disease, because it does not improve long-term outcomes while it does increase the risk of recurrent laryngeal nerve injury and hypoparathyroidism. For larger cN0 tumors it may be considered, with limited evidence. Therapeutic dissection remains indicated when nodal involvement is identified, and ipsilateral central dissection is recommended when lateral neck nodal disease is present.

Why the others fail:
(B) An honest argument, and the guidelines answer it directly: the staging information gained does not change outcomes enough to justify the morbidity in this group.
(C) This option states something true. Occult central nodal metastases are found in up to half of clinically node-negative papillary carcinoma patients eligible for lobectomy. That prevalence is real, and it is why the operation feels justified in the moment. It still does not follow, because most of that occult disease never becomes clinically relevant while every dissection carries a nerve and parathyroid risk that is immediate and sometimes permanent.
(D) Misunderstands post-lobectomy surveillance. After lobectomy, serial thyroglobulin monitoring is not recommended, because the remaining lobe produces it. Ultrasound every one to three years for five to eight years is the follow-up, not a thyroglobulin trend.

Keypoint: prevalence is not benefit, which is the same reasoning error you met at Steps 4, 5 and 6, in its final and most surgical form.

Debriefing question for the group: her husband asked a reasonable question and the answer is no. How do you say that in a way he accepts?

Reference: Ringel MD, Sosa JA, Baloch Z, et al. 2025 American Thyroid Association Management Guidelines for Adult Patients with Differentiated Thyroid Cancer. Thyroid. 2025;35(8):841-985, Recommendations 19 and 20.
